name: Lakshmi Devi Temple
significance: A soapstone shrine completed about 1113 by the merchant Kalhana Ravuta and his wife Sahaja Devi in the reign of Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, it is one of the earliest dated Hoysala temples and ranges four sanctums - Mahalakshmi, Kali, Shiva and Vishnu - around a shared hall inside a nine-shrine compound.

name: Bucesvara Temple
significance: A two-shrine (dvikuta) temple raised in 1173 by the wealthy officer Buci to mark the coronation of Hoysala king Veera Ballala II, its second sanctum given to Surya. Koravangala was a busy twelfth-century town with at least six temples, several endowed by Buci's brothers.

name: Lakshminarasimha Temple
significance: A three-shrine Hoysala temple of the mid-thirteenth century under Vira Someshwara, with subsidiary sanctums for Sridhara and Venugopala. Lacking a foundation stone, it is dated from sculptors' signatures, among them the master Mallitamma, and carries over a hundred carved panels.

name: Lakshminarayana Temple
significance: A soapstone three-shrine temple of 1250 built under Hoysala king Vira Someshwara, with side sanctums for Venugopala and Lakshmi Narasimha. Its four-storey vesara tower and plinth friezes of the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana mark the late Hoysala manner.

name: Mallikarjuna Temple
significance: Built about 1234 by the officer Harihara Dhannayaka during the reign of Hoysala king Vira Narasimha II, this three-shrine temple on a raised jagati keeps a stellate tower over its central sanctum and is protected as a monument of national importance.

name: Cheluvanarayana Swamy Temple
significance: Established by Ramanujacharya after he became preceptor at the Hoysala court, with the image installed in 1099 and the temple completed in 1104 on a grant of 5,000 gadyanas from Vishnuvardhana; later Mysore rulers endowed it with jewelled crowns.
story: Ramanuja is said to have recovered the stolen processional image from the Delhi sultan's court, where the sultan's daughter had grown so attached to it that she merged with the deity and is honoured as Bibi Nachiyar.

name: Panchakuta Basadi
significance: A Jain complex of shrines to Adinatha, Shantinatha and Neminatha built in two phases under the Western Gangas and renovated by the Hoysalas; scholars date it between the eighth and tenth centuries. The village takes its name from the free-standing Brahmadeva pillar before the shrines.

name: Chennakeshava Temple
significance: A compact single-shrine temple of about 1250 built under Hoysala king Vira Someshwara, its sixteen-pointed star plan and tiered shikhara making it a much-cited example of mature Hoysala workmanship. It is a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Harihareshwara Temple
significance: Built in 1223-24 by Polalva, a commander of Hoysala king Vira Narasimha II, with further work in 1268, the temple enshrines Harihara, a single image joining Shiva's right half to Vishnu's left. Old Kannada inscriptions and hero stones stand in its precinct; the original tower has been replaced in brick.
story: A demon named Guha is said to have terrorised the region until Vishnu and Shiva combined as Harihara and destroyed him, descending at nearby Kudalur where the Tungabhadra meets the Haridra.

name: Teru Malleshvara Temple
significance: A Vijayanagara-period Shiva temple of about 1466 in Hiriyur town, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and known for interior murals of scenes from the Hindu epics. A week-long jatra is held at the Magha full moon.

name: Someshwara Temple
significance: An ornate granite and stucco temple in Kolar town, assigned by the Archaeological Survey of India to the early fourteenth century though the art historian George Michell reads it as roughly seventeenth century. It is protected as a monument of national importance.

name: Kasivisvesvara Temple
significance: A twin-sanctum temple facing a smaller Surya shrine across a shared platform, generally dated between the early eleventh and mid twelfth centuries and counted among the fullest statements of the Kalyana Chalukya idiom that fuses Nagara, Dravida and Vesara forms. Hoysala king Ballala II reaffirmed the site's standing in 1192.

name: Someshwara Temple
significance: A Kalyani Chalukya monument in Lakshmeshwara whose records indicate it began as a Jain temple before passing to Shaiva worship; the sanctum image shows Shiva seated on Nandi. The Archaeological Survey of India restored the building between 2012 and 2015 with support from the Infosys Foundation.

name: Siddhesvara Temple
significance: A soapstone temple of the late eleventh century, unusual in facing west, whose original dedication is debated: loose sculptures and damaged wall images suggest it may have served Vaishnava and Jain worship before becoming Shaiva. Inscriptions of 1087 and 1108 survive within it, and a 1067 record names Haveri as an old centre of learning.

name: Tarakeshwara Temple
significance: Built of grey-green chloritic schist by the Chalukyas of Kalyana, with shrines for Nandi and Ganesha and three inscribed memorial stones in Kannada. It is listed by the Archaeological Survey of India and shows Hoysala influence in its detailing.

name: Kedareshvara Temple
significance: A soapstone temple of the late eleventh century with inscribed additions by the Hoysalas down to 1131, holding lingas in two shrines and a Vishnu image in the third. Balligavi was a leading Western Chalukya town and a centre of the Kalamukha Shaiva order; the temple is now a monument of national importance.
story: Some inscriptions at the site connect the temple with the legend of the demon Bali.

name: Kaitabheshvara Temple
significance: Built around 1100 in the reign of the Hoysala king Vinayaditya, a feudatory of the Western Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI, this soapstone temple also carries images of Mahishamardini, Bhairava and Ganesha and an old Kannada inscription of the 1240s in its hall.

name: Humcha Jain Temples
significance: The chief Jain centre of the Santara dynasty, founded in the seventh century, where the Padmavati shrine was rebuilt by Vira Santara in 1061 and the surviving Panchakuta Basadi raised in 1077 by Chattaladevi. It remained a major pilgrimage site until Hoysala patronage shifted to Vaishnavism in the twelfth century.
story: Prince Jinadatta of Mathura is said to have fled assassination carrying a golden image of Padmavati and, after a dream beneath a tree, founded Pombuccapura - today's Humcha - and its shrines to Parshvanatha and Padmavati.

name: Kanakachalapathi Temple
significance: A sixteenth-century Vishnu temple raised by a local Vijayanagara-era chief at Kanakagiri, the ancient Swarnagiri, with wide pillared halls, massive yali columns and three tiered gopuras. It is a protected monument under the state division of the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Kamala Narayana Temple
significance: A three-celled Kadamba temple of 1174 near Kittur, commissioned by Queen Kamala Devi, wife of King Sivachitta Permadi, and built by her chief architect Tippoja. Its ceiling carries a huge inverted lotus and its panels bear Kadamba dynastic emblems.

name: Kamal Basadi
significance: A Jain temple inside Belgaum fort built about 1204 by Birchiraja, an officer of the Ratta ruler Kartavirya IV, under the guidance of the monk Subhachandrabhattarakadeva; its black image of Neminatha stands beneath a carved lotus ceiling. Inscriptions of 1205 recording further work are now with the Royal Asiatic Society in Mumbai.

name: Banavasi Madhukeshwara Temple
significance: The principal shrine of Banavasi, the old Kadamba capital in Uttara Kannada, attributed to the Kadamba dynasty and among the earliest temple foundations in the region. Mahashivaratri and the Banavasi fair are its main observances.

name: Chaturmukha Basadi
significance: A four-faced Jain shrine of 1562 built in the reign of Rani Chennabhairadevi, the long-ruling queen of Gerusoppa known as the Pepper Queen. Gerusoppa was a Jain capital under the Saluva chiefs, and this is one of only a handful of its temples still standing.

name: Kanaganahalli Mahastupa
significance: Excavations between 1994 and 2002 uncovered a large brick and limestone stupa with sculptured drum slabs, Buddha images and 145 inscriptions, including a portrait panel labelled Raya Asoko - a rare contemporary depiction of the emperor Ashoka. Its carving sits between the earlier Amaravati and later Nagarjunakonda manners.

name: Kodandarama Temple
significance: A large sixteenth-century temple in Kadapa district whose sanctum holds Rama, Sita and Lakshmana carved from a single block of stone. It grew through several building phases, drew the notice of the traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, and is tied to the Telugu devotional tradition of Annamacharya; the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams took over its administration in 2015.
story: The town is said to be named for two devotees of Rama, Vontudu and Mittudu, who are remembered as having raised the shrine and received the god's grace on finishing it.

name: Madhavaraya Temple
significance: A temple within the fort of Gandikota in Kadapa district, dated by its carving to the first quarter of the sixteenth century and recorded in contemporary inscriptions naming donors who offered garlands to the god. It is designated a Monument of National Importance.

name: Pushpagiri Temple Complex
significance: A cluster of shrines on the Penna in Kadapa district, largely Shaiva and headed by the Vaidyanatheswara temple, whose core goes back to about the seventh century. Rashtrakuta, Kakatiya and Vijayanagara rulers all endowed it, and its inscriptions span several centuries.
story: Garuda is said to have spilled a drop of amrita into the lake here while freeing his mother, and the mound of flowers left by Rama's worship is held to have given Pushpagiri its name.

name: Chintalarayaswami Temple
significance: A mid-sixteenth-century Vijayanagara temple at Tadipatri built by the chief Pemmasani Timmanayudu II, a Monument of National Importance whose stone Garuda mandapa is carved as a chariot with turning granite wheels, in the manner of the Vitthala temple at Hampi.
story: The presiding image is said to have been found in a tamarind tree - chinta in Telugu - which gave the god the name Chintala Venkataramana.

name: Bugga Ramalingeswara Swamy Temple
significance: Built between 1490 and 1509 by Pemmasani Ramalinga Nayudu I, a chief of the Gutti-Gandikota country, on the south bank of the Penna at Tadipatri. Its walls carry reliefs of Ramayana and Mahabharata episodes, the west-facing linga is held to be swayambhu, and a row of slender pillars sounds the seven notes when struck. The temple's history is recorded in the Tadipatri kaifiyat collected by Colin Mackenzie in 1802.

name: Govindaraja Temple
significance: One of the largest and earliest temple complexes in Tirupati town, consecrated by Ramanuja in 1130 in the Vaikhanasa tradition, with older structures of the ninth and tenth centuries inside the enclosure. The town of Kotturu grew around it and was absorbed into the city; it is administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
story: During raids on the Govindaraja Perumal temple at Chidambaram the processional image is said to have been brought here for safekeeping and returned once the danger had passed.

name: Vedanarayana Temple
significance: One of the few Indian temples where Vishnu is worshipped in his Matsya form. For three days each year the rising sun runs the length of the temple from the gopuram to the sanctum, touching the deity's feet, navel and crown on successive mornings. It is administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.

name: Kalyana Venkateswara Temple
significance: Established in 1541 and extended later, this temple in Narayanavanam follows Vaikhanasa Agama in its daily worship and is administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams.
story: Narayanavanam is remembered as the capital of King Akasaraja, who is said to have given his daughter Padmavati in marriage to Venkateswara here before the god withdrew to Tirumala.

name: Pallikondeswara Temple
significance: A rare shrine where Shiva is shown reclining with his head on Parvati's lap, built under the Vijayanagara ruler Harihara Bukka Raya in the 1340s, renovated by a princess of Kalahasti in 1833 and reconsecrated in 2002.
story: Worn out after swallowing the poison churned from the ocean, Shiva is said to have rested his head on Parvati's lap at this spot while the gods waited for him to recover.

name: Kukkuteswara Temple
significance: The main Shaiva temple of Pithapuram, which also houses the shrine of Puruhutika Devi, counted among the eighteen maha shakti pithas. Pithapuram itself is named in the Skanda Purana, in Srinatha's fifteenth-century Bhimeswara Puranamu and in Samudragupta's Prayaga pillar inscription of about 350 CE; a monolithic Nandi stands before the sanctum.

name: Bhavanarayana Temple
significance: Thirty-two inscriptions of the eleventh to fourteenth centuries record the patronage of this red-stone temple, the earliest of 1073 endowing a perpetual lamp; donors include the Eastern Chalukyas, the Chola king Kulottunga I and the Reddi ruler Kataya Vema in 1414. The poet Srinatha names it in the fifteenth century.
story: The Brahma Vaivarta Purana tells that the serpent Ananta did penance here for Vishnu's protection, and that Vishnu promised to dwell at the place with Lakshmi, naming it Sarpapura.

name: Sri Talpagiri Ranganadha Swamy Temple
significance: One of the oldest temples of Nellore, standing on the bank of the Penna and believed to date from the twelfth century; its roughly seventy-foot gopuram, crowned with gilded kalashams, was built by Yeragudipati Venkatachalam Panthulu. The annual Brahmotsavam falls in March or April.

name: Tripuranthakeswara Temple
significance: A hill temple on the Guntur-Srisailam road in Markapuram district whose linga is worshipped as Bala Tripurantakeswara; it is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams sung by the Tamil saint Appar. The Bala Tripura Sundari shrine about two kilometres away is regarded as the eastern gateway of Srisailam.

name: Veerabhadra Temple
significance: A twelfth-century temple attributed to the Reddi kings, standing on the Devakuta hill on an islet in the Godavari and counted in the Skanda Purana among the five Kasi kshetras.
story: After Sati burned herself at Daksha's sacrifice, Shiva is said to have brought forth Veerabhadra and Bhadrakali; Veerabhadra beheaded Daksha and danced the Rudra Tandava here until sage Agastya calmed him and Shiva settled as a linga at the spot.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Temple
significance: A hill temple near Guntur patronised by the Vijayanagara rulers, with an inscription recording a visit by Krishnadevaraya. Its eleven-storey gopuram, about 153 feet high, was raised by Raja Vasireddy Venkatadri Nayudu of Amaravathi and is among the tallest in south India.
story: Tradition holds that the shrine was discovered by Yudhishthira, eldest of the Pandava brothers.

name: Alampur Navabrahma Temples
significance: Nine Shiva temples built by the Badami Chalukyas near the meeting of the Tungabhadra and Krishna, early experiments that set northern Nagara forms beside the Karnata Dravida manner and carry Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta imagery. Damaged from the fourteenth century onward, they were restored by the Archaeological Survey of India after 1980, and the Sangameswara temple was moved by 1990 ahead of submergence by the Srisailam dam.

name: Jogulamba Temple
significance: One of the eighteen maha shakti pithas, sharing its compound with the Navabrahma temples on the Tungabhadra. The seventh-century original was destroyed in 1390 during Bahmani raids; the shrine was rebuilt in 2005 and the old image reinstalled, and the site was later taken into the government's PRASAD pilgrimage scheme.
story: The place is held to be where the upper teeth of Sati fell after Daksha's sacrifice.

name: Chaya Someswara Temple
significance: A three-shrine temple at Panagal built under the Kunduru Chodas around the middle of the eleventh century, with subsidiary sanctums for Vishnu and Surya. Its pillars are set so that a shadow falls constantly across the linga through the day, giving the temple its name; it was restored after falling into ruin in the twentieth century.

name: Komrelly Mallanna Temple
deity: Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy, a form of Shiva)
significance: A hill shrine in Siddipet district about 85 km from Hyderabad, one of the main centres of the folk worship of Mallanna, whom devotees also identify with Khandoba.
story: The Oggu Katha singers tell how Mallanna won the goddess Medallamma by meeting the conditions set by her brothers.

name: Sri Ujjaini Mahakali Temple
significance: Founded in 1815 by Suriti Appaiah, a doli bearer posted with a military battalion moved from Secunderabad to Ujjain, who vowed a shrine if a cholera outbreak ended; he installed a wooden image on his return in 1814 and the temple grew around it. It is the focus of the Bonalu festival in the twin cities.

name: Kondagattu Anjaneya Swamy Temple
significance: A hill temple in Jagtial district that has been a centre of Hanuman worship for several centuries by local tradition; devotees keep a forty-day round of worship there.

name: Kota Gullu
significance: A walled group of some twenty-two stone temples to Shiva raised under the Kakatiya king Ganapatideva, nine kilometres from the Ramappa temple near Warangal; an inscription records a donation of 1234-35. The complex was heavily damaged, either in raids between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries or by a seventeenth-century earthquake.

name: Neelakantheswara Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple in Nizamabad town that draws large crowds at Shivaratri.
story: The Puranas are said to record that Brahma himself worshipped the linga enshrined here.

name: Sanghi Temple
significance: Completed in 1991 on the Paramanand Giri hill some 35 km from Hyderabad and built by the Sanghi family as a version of the Tirumala temple, its tall raja gopuram visible for kilometres around.

name: Koodalmanikyam Temple
significance: The only ancient Indian temple dedicated to Bharata and one of the four Kerala nalambalam shrines to the brothers of the Ramayana; a stone inscription of the Chera Perumal king Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara dated 854-55 shows it already existed. Its hereditary head, the Thachudaya Kaimal, held both spiritual and temporal authority over wide estates until 1971.
story: The temple tank Kulipini Theertham is held to have been sanctified by the sage Kulipini, who performed a great yajna at the spot.

name: Thriprayar Temple
significance: A well-known Rama temple on the bank of the Triprayar river in Thrissur district, whose name is read as 'the sacred river before the temple'. The waterway beside it later became part of Kerala's inland canal system.
story: The image is said to have been worshipped by Krishna at Dwaraka, cast into the sea after his departure, and recovered centuries later by a fisherman who brought it ashore here.

name: Peruvanam Mahadeva Temple
significance: A seven-acre temple near Cherpu counted among Kerala's 108 Shiva shrines, unusual in holding two lingas of different size in one sanctum, with Parvati worshipped in the same chamber and a 120-foot shrine to Madathilappan. It is the centre of the Peruvanam Pooram, at which the deities of nineteen neighbouring temples come to pay homage.
story: A sage named Puru is said to have done penance in this forest, so that the place came to be called Peruvanam.

name: Chengannur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A major Shiva temple near the Pamba in Alappuzha district, ranked with Ettumanoor, Vaikom and Vadakkunnathan among Kerala's great Shaiva shrines and administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board; the goddess is enshrined behind the linga facing west.
story: Parvati is said to have come here after her marriage and to have observed her monthly seclusion for twenty-eight days before granting darshan to sage Agastya - the origin of the rare Thripputhu observance, when the temple closes for three days.

name: Haripad Sree Subrahmanya Swamy Temple
builtDisplay: rebuilt in the 20th c. after a fire
significance: One of the oldest and largest Subrahmanya temples in Kerala, with four gopurams, a round sanctum, a golden flag mast and a koothambalam; it was rebuilt in the twentieth century under the Travancore ruler Sree Chithira Thirunal Rama Varma after fire destroyed the earlier structure.
story: The four-armed image is said to have been found in the Kayamkulam lake after landlords of Eakachakra shared the same vision, and Vishnu himself is said to have appeared as a saint to consecrate it, giving the place the name Harigeethapuram, today's Haripad.

name: Thirunakkara Sree Mahadevar Temple
significance: The principal Shiva temple of Kottayam town, built about five centuries ago by the Maharaja of Thekkumkur in traditional Kerala style.
story: An ageing Thekkumkur king who could no longer travel to Vadakkumnathan is said to have been promised the god's presence at home; after a dream, his servants found a bleeding swayambhu linga at Nakkarakkunnu, and he raised the temple over it.

name: Thirumandhamkunnu Temple
significance: The state shrine of the Valluvanad kings at Angadipuram, from which their Nair warriors set out for the Mamankam; its eleven-day Pooram in March-April draws pilgrims from across Malabar.
story: King Mandhata is said to have received a linga from Shiva at Kailasa, which fixed itself into this hill; when Parvati sent Bhadrakali and her hosts to reclaim it, a fifteen-day struggle with the king's ascetics ended with the linga splitting and the deities merging into it.

name: Triprangode Siva Temple
significance: An old pilgrimage centre in Malappuram district with inscriptions of the Later Chera ruler Goda Ravi Varma of the tenth century and mentions in fifteenth-century texts; its two-storeyed shrine is built in the apsidal gajaprishta form. It served as a military camp during fourteenth-century conflicts and was later tied to the Kingdom of Tanur.
story: Shiva is said to have burst from the linga here to save the boy sage Markandeya from Yama, and is worshipped in that form as Kalasamhara Murti.

name: Kottiyoor Temple
significance: Two shrines facing each other across the Vavali river inside an eighty-acre sacred forest in Kannur district: the permanent Thruchherumana temple on the west bank, raised over a swayambhu linga, and a temporary eastern shrine opened only for the 27-day Vysakha Mahotsavam. It is managed by the Malabar Devaswom Board.
story: The eastern bank is held to be the place where Daksha's sacrifice ended and Sati gave up her life, which is why the site is counted among the origins of the Shakti Peethas.

name: Thiruvangad Sree Ramaswami Temple
significance: One of Kerala's five principal Rama temples, known to the English as the Brass Pagoda for its copper-sheeted roof. It stood as an outpost of Thalassery fort, was damaged during Tipu Sultan's eighteenth-century campaigns, and hosted talks between East India Company officers and local chiefs.

name: Ananthapura Lake Temple
significance: The only lake temple in Kerala, standing at the centre of a two-acre tank in Kasaragod district, with Vishnu seated on the five-hooded serpent Anantha, a wooden ceiling carved with the ten avatars and painted navagrahas. The original images, made of medicinal materials, were replaced with panchaloha in 1972.
story: Sage Vilwamangalam is said to have been visited here by Narayana in the form of a child who vanished into a cave when scolded; following him southward, the sage found him become a tree in the shape of Vishnu reclining on the serpent, the deity having moved on to Thiruvananthapuram.

name: Madhur Temple
significance: A three-tiered apsidal temple in Kasaragod district whose woodwork carries scenes of Ganesha and the Ramayana; the linga is said to have been found by a woman named Madaru of the Tulu Moger community, and the Ganapathi figure drawn on the sanctum wall by a boy grew to overshadow the older dedication. It was long held by the Kumbla rajas of Maipady Palace before passing to the Devaswom board.
story: Tipu Sultan is said to have come to demolish the temple but to have changed his mind after drinking water from its well, leaving only a sword mark on the well house.

name: Tali Shiva Temple
significance: One of the oldest temples of Kozhikode, built in the fourteenth century by the Zamorin and closely bound to his court; its two-storeyed sanctum is shaped like a chariot. Damaged during Tipu Sultan's eighteenth-century invasion, it was renovated in 1964.
story: The linga in the sanctum is said to have been installed by Parasurama at the close of the Dvapara Yuga.

name: Viswanatha Swamy Temple
significance: An early fifteenth-century Shiva temple on the bank of the Kalpathy river, endowed by Ittikombi Achan of the Palakkad royal family in an inscription of Malayalam Era 600 (1424-25) and ringed by four Tamil Brahmin agraharams. Its likeness to the Kashi Viswanatha temple at Varanasi earned it the name Dakshina Kashi, and it is the centre of the annual Kalpathi Ratholsavam.
story: Lakshmi Ammal of Kollengode is remembered as having carried a Shiva linga home from Varanasi and installed it here with the Raja of Palakkad's support, endowing 1,320 gold coins for its upkeep.

name: Aluva Mahadeva Temple
significance: A temple on the sand bank of the Periyar at Aluva, counted among Kerala's 108 Shiva shrines and unusual in having no sreekovil: the linga rises directly from the riverbed sand, which is why the Sivaratri gathering on the Aluva Manalpuram is held in the open.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the image here.
